What does a static route say, in plain English? Give the syntax.

'To reach this network, send to this neighbor.'
ip route <network> <mask> <next hop>
Example: ip route 192.168.3.0 255.255.255.0 192.168.2.2
A ping from R1 to a remote server works, but a ping from a PC behind R1 fails. What's the likely cause?
The far side has no return route to the PC's LAN. R1's own ping uses its exit interface IP as the source, which the far router reaches through a connected route.
PC LAN 192.168.10.0/24 - R1 - 10.0.0.0/30 - R2 - Server LAN 172.16.5.0/24. R1 is 10.0.0.1, R2 is 10.0.0.2. R1 has a route to 172.16.5.0/24 via 10.0.0.2. PC-to-server pings fail. Fix, and where?

On R2: ip route 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.1
The request gets there; the reply has no way back.
In that same setup, why can't R2's route to 192.168.10.0/24 point at 192.168.10.1 (R1's LAN interface)?
R2 has to reach the next hop directly, on a network it's connected to. 192.168.10.1 is on the far side of R1, so R2 can't hand it a packet.
R1's WAN interface is 10.0.0.1/30 and R1 has only connected routes. You add ip route 172.16.5.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.0.6. Is it installed?
No. 10.0.0.6 isn't in 10.0.0.0/30 (0-3), and R1 has no other route to it, so the next hop can't be resolved. It sits in the config, not the table.
Write a static route to 192.168.3.0/24 through R2 (192.168.2.2) out Gi0/0/0, three different ways.
With an exit-interface-only static route on Ethernet, who does the router ARP for?

The final destination itself, as if it were directly connected. It only works because the next router answers on its behalf (proxy ARP). That's why next-hop or fully specified is preferred on Ethernet.
Write a default route to an ISP router at 203.0.113.1.
The mask makes it a route to the single address 0.0.0.0, not a catch-all. A default route needs mask 0.0.0.0.
Your ISP assigns you 203.0.113.10/30. What has to be the next hop for your default route?
203.0.113.9. The /30 is 203.0.113.8-11; the only usable addresses are .9 and .10, and you're .10.
Your ISP assigns you 198.51.100.6/30. What's the ISP's address?
198.51.100.5. The /30 is .4-.7, usable .5 and .6, and you're .6.
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 216.0.5.1 is configured, but the interface on 216.0.5.0/30 is shut down. Is the default route in the routing table?
No. The router can't resolve the next hop (there's no connected route to 216.0.5.0/30), so the static route stays in the config but isn't installed. Gateway of last resort: not set.
A default route is configured, but show ip route says 'Gateway of last resort is not set'. Likely cause?
The route isn't installed because its next hop can't be resolved, usually because the ISP-facing interface is down or misaddressed.
How does a default route appear in show ip route?
S* 0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via <next hop>, plus 'Gateway of last resort is <next hop>' at the top. The * marks it as the candidate default.
When does a router use the default route?
Only when nothing more specific matches. /0 is the least specific route possible.
You configure ip default-gateway 203.0.113.1 on a router with routing enabled. Does it get internet access?
No. A router with routing on ignores ip default-gateway. It needs ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1.
R1 - R2 - R3 in a line, with a LAN on R1 and a LAN on R3. Using only specific static routes, what's the minimum needed for the two LANs to reach each other?

4.
R1: a route to R3's LAN.
R2: routes to both LANs (it's connected to neither).
R3: a route to R1's LAN.
Two static routes to 10.5.0.0/16, one via 192.168.2.2 and one via 192.168.4.2, both resolvable. What does the router do?
Installs both and load-balances across them. Same prefix, same AD, same metric.
What's a floating static route?
A static route given a worse (higher) AD than the route it backs up, like ip route 10.5.0.0 255.255.0.0 192.168.4.2 200. It stays out of the table until the main route disappears.
A static route to 10.5.0.0/16 is configured with AD 130. OSPF also learns 10.5.0.0/16. Which is installed?
OSPF's (AD 110). 110 beats 130. Raising a static route's AD can make it lose.
A static route to 10.5.0.0/16 is configured with AD 100. OSPF also learns 10.5.0.0/16. Which is installed?
The static route. 100 beats OSPF's 110.
How do you remove the static route to 192.168.3.0/24?
no ip route 192.168.3.0 255.255.255.0 (the next hop is optional when removing).
R1 can ping R2's WAN address but nothing on R2's LAN, and no routing is configured on R1. Why?
R1 only knows its connected networks. It has no route to R2's LAN, so it drops those packets.
A static route's next hop is on a directly connected network, and that interface goes down. What happens to the static route?
It's removed from the table (the next hop can't be resolved anymore) and comes back when the interface comes up. It stays in the running config the whole time.
R1 has a static route through R2. R2's link to the remote LAN fails, but R1's link to R2 stays up. What happens to R1's static route?
Nothing. It stays installed and keeps sending traffic to R2, which drops it. Static routes don't know about failures past the next hop.
